title: India and EU Race to Sign Free Trade Deal at Modi's December Brussels Visit
excerpt: With negotiations concluded in January, the race is now procedural: a Commission fast-track, a Council vote in early December, and a signature timed to Modi's Brussels trip.
body:
• India and the European Union are racing to sign their free trade agreement in Brussels around December 16-18, timed to a visit by Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
  • Negotiations concluded in January 2026; the European Commission has proposed a fast-track approval so legal and translation delays do not push signature into 2027.
  • The deal — billed by Brussels as the 'mother of all deals' — would eliminate or reduce tariffs on more than 90% of EU goods exported to India and cover markets of about two billion people.
  • Signature is not entry into force: the Council of the EU and the European Parliament must still approve, and India must ratify. Sensitive farm goods including dairy, sugar, beef and rice are excluded.

India and the European Union are in a final sprint to sign their long-negotiated free trade agreement before the end of December, with a signing window emerging in Brussels around December 17 or 18 to coincide with an expected visit by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. According to Ei Samay and agency reporting, both sides want the pact signed before the December deadline, and Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal has just concluded a two-day visit to Germany as part of a six-day Germany-Netherlands tour to deepen economic ties.

Why December, and why fast-track

The negotiations themselves are done — they were concluded on January 27, 2026, at the 16th India-EU summit in New Delhi, after a process first launched in 2007, suspended in 2013 and relaunched in 2022. What remains is the signature, and the calendar is tight. Rapporteur reports Modi is scheduled to visit Brussels on December 16, a day before EU leaders gather on December 17-18, and that Tomas Baert, trade adviser to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, confirmed the visit is expected to provide the occasion for the formal signing. The Commission put its signature proposals to the Council on September 11, 2026, opting for a fast-track procedure based on the English text rather than waiting for translations into all 24 official EU languages — an approach some member states have questioned, according to diplomatic sources cited by Ei Samay. EU ambassadors and ministers have not yet authorised the signing; approval could come in early December.

What is in — and out of — the deal

Brussels has repeatedly called the pact the "mother of all deals": bilateral goods trade was €120 billion in 2024, and the agreement would eliminate tariffs on over 90 per cent of tariff lines. But the exclusions matter as much as the coverage. The agreement does not liberalise sensitive agricultural products on either side, including dairy, sugar, beef and rice, and energy, raw materials and government procurement are largely absent. The trade and sustainable development chapter is less ambitious than in other EU deals, and the Paris Agreement is not an essential element, meaning the pact cannot be suspended solely over a climate withdrawal.

What it means for the diaspora

Beyond goods, the package is paired with a mobility framework that both sides say will ease movement for skilled Indian professionals into the EU, and a separate investment agreement is being worked on in parallel. For Indian exporters — and for diaspora-run businesses trading between Europe and India — the practical change starts only after ratification, but a December signature locks in the text and starts the parliamentary clock in Brussels.

What happens next

The sequence is now precise: a Council authorisation decision in early December, signature during Modi's Brussels visit around December 16-18, then European Parliament consent — a step diplomats estimate adds one to two months — and ratification in India before the agreement can enter into force. EU leaders António Costa and Ursula von der Leyen told Modi at the G7 sidelines in Evian in June that they wanted the deal signed by year-end; the December window is the last scheduled one that fits.
